calib.name: prose_en
calib.text: The lighthouse keeper climbed the spiral stairs every evening at dusk, counting the one hundred and twelve steps as he had done for thirty years. From the top he could see the fishing boats returning to the harbour, their lamps swinging like slow fireflies over the dark water. He lit the great lamp, checked the clockwork that turned it, and wrote the weather in his log: wind from the north-west, sea moderate, visibility good. His daughter had asked him once why he still kept the log by hand when the automatic station recorded everything. He told her that the sea did not care about the station, but it might, one day, care about him.

calib.text: 清晨的雾还没有散去，老街上的早点铺已经开始忙碌。蒸笼里冒出白色的热气，和路边的雾混在一起，分不清哪一缕来自锅里，哪一缕来自天上。骑车上班的人停下来买两个包子，付钱的时候和老板聊几句天气。孩子们背着书包跑过石板路，鞋底敲出清脆的声音。这样的早晨在这条街上重复了几十年，没有人觉得它特别，也没有人希望它改变。

calib.name: history_en
calib.text: The printing press changed how knowledge moved through Europe. Before it, a book was a rare object copied by hand over months; after it, the same text could exist in hundreds of towns within a year. Prices fell, literacy rose, and arguments that had once stayed inside a monastery or a court spread to merchants, craftsmen and students. Governments and churches tried to control what was printed, but the number of presses grew faster than the number of censors. Historians still debate how much of the scientific revolution depended on print, but few doubt that it made results easier to check and harder to suppress.

eval.name: prose_eval
eval.text: In the small workshop behind the market, the clockmaker kept every broken watch that customers had abandoned. He said each one had stopped at a moment that mattered to somebody, and that a watch which had stopped could still be honest about the time it remembered. His apprentice thought this was sentimental until the day she opened a pocket watch that had stopped at four minutes past two and found, folded inside the case, a train ticket dated forty years earlier.
